scenes.visual: Title card: One Route to Speech.

scenes.tts: In eighteen sixty-one, a man named Luh-born-yuh could say almost nothing beyond one syllable. Yet he appeared to follow much of what was said to him. What exactly had broken?
scenes.caption: In 1861, a man named Leborgne could say almost nothing beyond one syllable. Yet he appeared to follow much of what was said to him. What exactly had broken?
scenes.visual: A nineteenth-century hospital ward, sketched. A speech bubble holds a single syllable. The question appears as on-screen text.
scenes.narration: In 1861, a man named Leborgne could say almost nothing beyond one syllable. Yet he appeared to follow much of what was said to him. What exactly had broken?

scenes.tts: Here is the idea. You can say only what reaches the language network of the speaking hemisphere, by an unbroken route.
scenes.visual: Rule card: You can say only what reaches the language network of the hemisphere that speaks, by an unbroken route.
scenes.narration: Here is the idea. You can say only what reaches the language network of the speaking hemisphere, by an unbroken route.

scenes.tts: Each bedside test travels part of that route. In this simple sketch, the pattern of what fails points to the broken stretch.
scenes.visual: The rule card shrinks to a corner. A dashed path appears with one stretch flashing. Corner label: simplified sketch.
scenes.narration: Each bedside test travels part of that route. In this simple sketch, the pattern of what fails points to the broken stretch.

scenes.tts: When you hear a word, both hemispheres analyse its sounds. Our route starts on the left, at the back of the superior temporal lobe. Here, roughly in Wernicke's area, the word's sound form is recognized.
scenes.visual: Both hemispheres seen from above: auditory regions glow faintly on both sides. Then the view turns to the left hemisphere from the side, where a spot at the back of the superior temporal lobe glows, labelled: sound form (roughly Wernicke's area).
scenes.narration: When you hear a word, both hemispheres analyse its sounds. Our route starts on the left, at the back of the superior temporal lobe. Here, roughly in Wernicke's area, the word's sound form is recognized.

scenes.tts: One road, the ventral, or lower, road, runs forward and down through the temporal lobe to meaning. It is how you understand spoon. Run backwards, it finds the sound form of a word you mean to say.
scenes.caption: One road, the ventral, or lower, road, runs forward and down through the temporal lobe to meaning. It is how you understand “spoon”. Run backwards, it finds the sound form of a word you mean to say.
scenes.visual: A path glows forward and down through the temporal lobe to a node labelled: meaning. A spoon icon appears. Small arrows then run along the same path in the opposite direction.
scenes.narration: One road, the ventral, or lower, road, runs forward and down through the temporal lobe to meaning. It is how you understand “spoon”. Run backwards, it finds the sound form of a word you mean to say.

scenes.tts: The other, the dorsal, or upper, road, runs up through parietal cortex to the frontal lobe. It links how a word sounds with how to say it.
scenes.visual: A second path glows up through parietal cortex and forward to the frontal lobe.
scenes.narration: The other, the dorsal, or upper, road, runs up through parietal cortex to the frontal lobe. It links how a word sounds with how to say it.

scenes.tts: There, roughly in Broca's area, a planner assembles the phrase and plans its movements: lips, tongue and larynx.
scenes.visual: A frontal node labelled: planner (roughly Broca's area). Small icons of lips, tongue and larynx appear beside it.
scenes.narration: There, roughly in Broca's area, a planner assembles the phrase and plans its movements: lips, tongue and larynx.

scenes.tts: Spontaneous speech starts from meaning, finds each word's sound form, and reaches the same planner by speech-generation connections of its own. The dorsal road adds support. The motor system then moves the muscles.
scenes.visual: A separate speech-generation arrow runs from meaning through sound form to the planner, distinct from the dorsal road, which glows faintly alongside it as support. The planner then feeds a separate box beyond the route, labelled: motor system (motor cortex, basal ganglia, cerebellum, brainstem). The box is marked: execution, outside the language network.
scenes.narration: Spontaneous speech starts from meaning, finds each word's sound form, and reaches the same planner by speech-generation connections of its own. The dorsal road adds support. The motor system then moves the muscles.

scenes.tts: In most people the dorsal road is strongly left-sided. Understanding single words gets help from both hemispheres.
scenes.visual: Both hemispheres seen from above. The dorsal road glows strongly on the left, with a faint partner on the right; the ventral road glows on both sides. Labels: strongly left-dominant dorsal road; ventral road on both sides.
scenes.narration: In most people the dorsal road is strongly left-sided. Understanding single words gets help from both hemispheres.

scenes.tts: A clinician runs four bedside tests. Each leans on a different part of the route.
scenes.visual: Four labels appear in a column: fluency, comprehension, repetition, naming.
scenes.narration: A clinician runs four bedside tests. Each leans on a different part of the route.

scenes.tts: Fluency is judged from the speech itself: phrase length, rate, effort and grammar. Several systems contribute. Comprehension links speech sounds with meaning.
scenes.visual: For fluency, the speech-generation network lights, with the frontal planner as one contributor among several. Then the sound-form-to-meaning stretch lights for comprehension.
scenes.narration: Fluency is judged from the speech itself: phrase length, rate, effort and grammar. Several systems contribute. Comprehension links speech sounds with meaning.

scenes.tts: Repetition runs from sound form along the dorsal road to the planner. Naming runs from a seen object to meaning, to the word's sound form, to the planner.
scenes.visual: The dorsal stretch lights for repetition. Then a pen icon feeds meaning, and the path from meaning to sound form to planner lights for naming.
scenes.narration: Repetition runs from sound form along the dorsal road to the planner. Naming runs from a seen object to meaning, to the word's sound form, to the planner.

scenes.tts: So damage at many stages can spoil naming. That is why naming rarely tells the syndromes apart.
scenes.visual: Small breaks appear in turn at meaning, at sound form and at the planner; naming fails at each one.
scenes.narration: So damage at many stages can spoil naming. That is why naming rarely tells the syndromes apart.

scenes.tts: In Broca aphasia, speech is slow and effortful. Comprehension is relatively preserved, but repetition is poor.
scenes.visual: On-screen text only, never spoken: “Boy ... cookie ... uh ... fall.” Label: composed for teaching.
scenes.narration: In Broca aphasia, speech is slow and effortful. Comprehension is relatively preserved, but repetition is poor.

scenes.tts: The break sits toward the frontal end, where the phrase is assembled and planned. Speech and repetition pass through it. Simple comprehension mostly does not.
scenes.visual: A damaged zone toward the frontal end of the route, reaching a little way back along it. The fluency and repetition stretches dim; comprehension stays lit. Small on-screen note: real lesions usually reach further.
scenes.narration: The break sits toward the frontal end, where the phrase is assembled and planned. Speech and repetition pass through it. Simple comprehension mostly does not.

scenes.tts: In Wernicke aphasia, speech flows but conveys little meaning. Words are swapped or invented.
scenes.visual: On-screen text only, never spoken: “the boy is over there doing the tooken, you know.” Label: composed for teaching.
scenes.narration: In Wernicke aphasia, speech flows but conveys little meaning. Words are swapped or invented.

scenes.tts: Comprehension and repetition both fail. The damage sits toward the start, where both roads begin, and touches several steps there.
scenes.visual: A broad damaged zone at the start of the route, where both roads begin. Both roads dim from their start. The speech-generation network stays lit and output flows, but the words it carries are marked wrong.
scenes.narration: Comprehension and repetition both fail. The damage sits toward the start, where both roads begin, and touches several steps there.

scenes.tts: Now you try. Suppose the dorsal road's link from sound to movement is impaired, but speech generation still works. Which tests suffer most?
scenes.visual: A break mark on the dorsal road only. The speech-generation arrow from meaning to the planner stays lit. The four test labels wait, unlit. The question appears as on-screen text.
scenes.narration: Now you try. Suppose the dorsal road's link from sound to movement is impaired, but speech generation still works. Which tests suffer most?

scenes.visual: The question stays on screen; a small countdown ring runs.

scenes.tts: Repetition fails most. Speech stays fluent, because speech generation still works, but sound errors creep in. Comprehension is relatively good. Naming often suffers too. This is conduction aphasia.
scenes.visual: Repetition turns red; naming turns amber; fluency and comprehension stay green. Label: conduction aphasia.
scenes.narration: Repetition fails most. Speech stays fluent, because speech generation still works, but sound errors creep in. Comprehension is relatively good. Naming often suffers too. This is conduction aphasia.

scenes.tts: Real words can sometimes be repeated with help from meaning, which still reaches the planner. Nonwords, like blick, lean on the dorsal road.
scenes.caption: Real words can sometimes be repeated with help from meaning, which still reaches the planner. Nonwords, like “blick”, lean on the dorsal road.
scenes.visual: For a real word, a detour arrow runs from sound form through meaning and along the speech-generation arrow to the planner. A nonword card, blick, has no detour: it needs the broken dorsal road, labelled: holds and maps the sounds.
scenes.narration: Real words can sometimes be repeated with help from meaning, which still reaches the planner. Nonwords, like “blick”, lean on the dorsal road.

scenes.tts: Suppose instead only the ventral road breaks, from sound form to meaning, and speech generation still works. What will she do?
scenes.visual: A break mark on the ventral road only. The question appears as on-screen text.
scenes.narration: Suppose instead only the ventral road breaks, from sound form to meaning, and speech generation still works. What will she do?

scenes.visual: The question stays on screen; a small countdown ring runs.

scenes.tts: Her speech stays fluent, but she understands poorly. Yet she can echo a sentence she does not understand. If the cut blocks traffic both ways, naming fails too, and her own speech grows empty. This is transcortical sensory aphasia.
scenes.visual: Comprehension turns red, then naming turns red as arrows on the ventral road stop in both directions; fluency and repetition stay green. Label: transcortical sensory aphasia.
scenes.narration: Her speech stays fluent, but she understands poorly. Yet she can echo a sentence she does not understand. If the cut blocks traffic both ways, naming fails too, and her own speech grows empty. This is transcortical sensory aphasia.

scenes.tts: Dysarthria is different. Weak or uncoordinated muscles slur speech. The damage lies in the motor system, beyond the language route. In isolated dysarthria, comprehension and writing are normal.
scenes.visual: A break mark inside the motor-system box beyond the route; the box lists motor cortex, basal ganglia, cerebellum, brainstem, nerves and muscles. The whole language route stays lit. Icons for listening and writing get check marks. Label: isolated dysarthria.
scenes.narration: Dysarthria is different. Weak or uncoordinated muscles slur speech. The damage lies in the motor system, beyond the language route. In isolated dysarthria, comprehension and writing are normal.

scenes.tts: The pattern of what fails points to a broken stretch of the route. It does not name one small patch of cortex.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: the pattern points to a stretch, not a patch. Small label: simplified sketch.
scenes.narration: The pattern of what fails points to a broken stretch of the route. It does not name one small patch of cortex.
